newsitem.title: USA: House-Senate panel approves disaster relief bill.
newsitem.headline: House-Senate panel approves disaster relief bill.

text.p: House and Senate negotiators Wednesday approved legislation to provide emergency relief to more than 30 disaster-stricken states, but President Clinton vowed to veto it unless unacceptable conditions were dropped.
Republicans rejected calls from Democrats for a stripped-down bill that just provided disaster aid for 35 states, including flood-stricken North Dakota, and funds to maintain U.S. troops in Bosnia.

Instead, the House-Senate conference panel kept controversial Republican-backed measures to avoid a government shut-down in case of another budget impasse between Congress and the White House, and to dictate how the government conducts the 2000 census.

"If the Republican majority is set on this course of adding contentious and extraneous provisions, they should send this bill as quickly as possible," Clinton said in a statement. "I will veto it as soon as it arrives."
The president said he will return the bill to Congress swiftly "so they can send me a clean disaster assistance bill immediately that keeps aid flowing to those in need."
"Americans in need should not have to endure this unnecessary delay," he said.
Republicans said they would be prepared to send another emergency spending bill to Clinton by early next week if he vetoed this one. The House and Senate were expected to vote on the bill Thursday.

The White House has said the government shut-down provision would remove incentives for Congress to negotiate on the budget, and a Republican call for the census to be done only by head counts, and without statistical sampling, would under-count minorities and poor people.
Earlier Wednesday, Republican leaders blocked Senate Democrats from holding an all night session in which they planned to lambaste Republicans for delaying the bill.
"They are shutting down the Senate just like they shut down the government. It is wrong," California Democratic Sen. Barbara Boxer told a news conference.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, a South Dakota Democrat, had called for the all night Senate session as a way to get the majority Republicans moving on the $8.4 billion spending bill. He had assigned himself the 3 a.m. to 6 a.m. EDT shift.
The bill provides $5 billion in disaster assistance for more than 30 states, $1.9 billion to pay for military operations in Bosnia and Iraq, and money for other government agencies.
"Our desire is to get this process moving. Let's at least get the veto over with," Daschle told reporters.
Republicans, who control the Senate floor by virtue of their 55-44 seat majority, moved to adjourn and prevented Democrats from taking the floor.

The collision course over the disaster relief holds political risks for both sides. Republicans said a veto would delay the assistance to flood-ravaged states even more while Democrats put the blame on Republicans since they have refused to allow votes on a non-controversial funding bill.
Mayors and business leaders of two communities hardest hit by this spring's floods -- Grand Forks, North Dakota, and East Grand Forks, Minnesota -- urged Congress to clear the aid.

"We have farmers in our states who can't plant; ranchers who are unable to renew their herds, and local school districts which are borrowing money right now to pay costs that should have already been covered by funds in this bill," the group said in a statement.
